newsitem.title: SUDAN: Judge named to draft new Sudanese constitution.
newsitem.headline: Judge named to draft new Sudanese constitution.

text.p: Sudanese President Omar Hassan al-Bashir has named former chief justice Khalafallah al-Rashid to lead the task of drafting a new constitution for the country, official sources said on Thursday.
Bashir took power through a military coup eight years ago, abolishing the existing multiparty system. He has ruled since then through interim constitutional arrangements.

A permanent constitution has been a longstanding aim of the Islamist-military government, especially since elections for a new parliament took place in 1996. The president has promised a popular referendum on the document once it is drafted.

At a meeting on Thursday with Rashid and two other newly appointed senior members of a constitutional commission, Bashir said the constitution should "meet the aspirations of the Sudanese people, with Islamic law and custom as its sources".
By custom he meant the traditional law of the southern Sudanese, mainly animists and Christians who reject the Islamic law the northerners have tried to impose on them.
The balance between sharia (Islamic law) and southern customary law is likely to be one of the most controversial aspects of debate on the new constitution.
The rebel Sudan People's Liberation Army, which has been fighting the government in the south since 1983, is opposed to any settlement which enforces sharia on non-Moslems.

Rashid, quoted by the official news agency SUNA, said he and his colleagues had instructions to accommodate all points of view. The new constitution should be "a model for national, political and social unity", he added.
Sudanese leaders have ruled out a return to the multiparty democratic system which Bashir overthrew.
They say the non-party system they have created is less divisive, but their opponents say it is just a device to prevent a serious challenge to Islamist domination of the government.
The government newspaper al-Anbaa said the commission was expected to have between 300 and 350 members, while a smaller technical committee would have 50 to 60 members.

The other senior members are Dafallah al-Radi, a former deputy chief justice, and Abbas Ibrahim al-Nour, a former ambassador to Libya and number two man in the Sudanese equivalent of a single ruling party. Nour will be rapporteur and Radi will be chairman of the technical committee.
SUNA said Bashir was leaving it to the three men to appoint the members of the commission. Al-Anbaa said he had told them that all parts of the country should be represented.
The commission has not been given a deadline for its work.
